answer: It moves changes from the working tree to the staging area.
explanation: git add stages changes: working tree to staging area. Only git commit records them in the repository, and only git push sends them to a remote. Deleting changes is what git restore does, not git add.
options: It commits changes to the remote repository.
It moves changes from the working tree to the staging area.
It downloads changes from the remote repository.
It permanently deletes unstaged changes.
title: Git three areas

answer: Rebase rewrites commit hashes, so teammates' copies diverge and need repair.
explanation: Rebasing replays commits as new commits with new hashes. Anyone who based work on the old commits now has divergent history. Rebase does handle conflicts, does not delete the branch, and works on any branch — the restriction is about shared history, not mechanics.
options: Rebase deletes the branch permanently.
Rebase rewrites commit hashes, so teammates' copies diverge and need repair.
Rebase cannot handle merge conflicts.
Rebase only works on the main branch.
prompt: Why should you not rebase a branch other developers have already based work on?
title: Merge vs rebase

answer: A container shares the host kernel and isolates processes with namespaces and cgroups.
explanation: The full guest OS on virtualised hardware is the virtual machine model. Containers share the host kernel, which is why they start in seconds and use less memory, and why a Linux container needs a Linux kernel.
options: A container runs a full guest operating system on virtualised hardware.
A container shares the host kernel and isolates processes with namespaces and cgroups.
A container cannot run a Java application.
A container is always slower to start than a virtual machine.
prompt: How does a container differ from a virtual machine?
title: Container vs virtual machine

answer: So dependency downloads are cached in their own layer and reused when only source code changes.
explanation: Docker reuses cached layers until an instruction's inputs change. Copying source first would invalidate the dependency layer on every code change and force a full re-download. There is no rule requiring pom.xml first, RUN can be followed by COPY, and multi-stage builds keep source out of the final image.
options: Because Docker requires pom.xml to be the first file copied.
So dependency downloads are cached in their own layer and reused when only source code changes.
Because source code cannot be copied after a RUN instruction.
Because it makes the final image contain the source code.
prompt: In a Dockerfile for a Maven project, why copy pom.xml and download dependencies before copying source code?
title: Docker layer caching

answer: Because pod IPs change when pods are replaced, so clients need a stable DNS name routing to current healthy pods.
explanation: Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs on replacement. A Service selects current healthy pods by label and gives them a stable name and virtual IP. Pods do have IPs, can start without a Service, and Services do not store data.
options: Because pods have no IP addresses at all.
Because pod IPs change when pods are replaced, so clients need a stable DNS name routing to current healthy pods.
Because a Service is required before any pod can start.
Because Services store the application's data.
prompt: Why does a Kubernetes Service exist, given that pods already have IP addresses?
title: Kubernetes Service purpose

answer: Because the artifact tested in staging must be the artifact that runs in production, or the testing proves nothing about it.
explanation: A rebuild can differ — different dependencies, timestamps, or build environment — so it is untested code. Promoting the same image guarantees what was tested is what ships. Rebuilding is possible and images can cross environments; the issue is correctness, not feasibility.
options: Because rebuilding is impossible in production.
Because the artifact tested in staging must be the artifact that runs in production, or the testing proves nothing about it.
Because images cannot be pulled across environments.
Because rebuilding would change the application's source code.
prompt: Why should the same container image travel through staging and production instead of rebuilding for production?
title: Build once, promote

answer: RDS with PostgreSQL, because it is a managed relational database matching JPA, joins, and transactions.
explanation: RDS provides managed PostgreSQL/MySQL that a JPA application talks to over JDBC. DynamoDB is a key-value store without SQL joins, S3 is object storage not a database, and ElastiCache is a cache, not durable relational storage.
options: DynamoDB, because it supports SQL joins natively.
RDS with PostgreSQL, because it is a managed relational database matching JPA, joins, and transactions.
S3, because it can store relational tables as objects.
ElastiCache, because it persists relational data permanently.
prompt: A Spring Boot service uses Spring Data JPA with joins and transactions. Which AWS database is the natural fit, and why?
title: RDS vs DynamoDB

description: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application built with Maven. The build stage must compile the jar, the runtime stage must contain only a JRE and the jar, dependencies must be cached before source is copied, and the container must run as a non-root user with an exec-form entrypoint exposing port 8080.
examples: Input: a Maven project with pom.xml and src/ → Output: an image that runs the Spring Boot jar on port 8080 without Maven or source code in the final image
hints: Copy pom.xml and download dependencies in their own layer before copying src/.
Use COPY --from=build to bring only the jar into the runtime stage.
Create a user and switch to it with USER before ENTRYPOINT.
solution:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/myapp-1.0.0.jar app.jar
RUN groupadd -r appgroup && useradd -r -g appgroup appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
title: Multi-stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot

description: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on pushes to main and on pull requests, sets up JDK 21 with a Maven cache, runs the full build and tests, then builds and pushes a container image tagged with the commit SHA. Secrets must not appear in the file.
examples: Input: a push to main → Output: build and tests run, then an image tagged with the commit SHA is pushed to the registry
hints: Trigger on push to main and on pull_request.
Use actions/setup-java with java-version 21 and cache maven.
Tag the image with github.sha so every image traces to one commit.
solution:
name: build-and-test
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up JDK 21
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: "21"
          distribution: temurin
          cache: maven
      - name: Build and test
        run: ./mvnw -q verify
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t <your-registry>/order-service:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push image
        run: docker push <your-registry>/order-service:${{ github.sha }}
title: CI pipeline for a Java service

description: Write a Kubernetes Deployment for a Spring Boot service named order-service with 3 replicas, a pinned image version, container port 8080, a prod Spring profile via environment variable, memory and CPU requests and limits, and liveness and readiness probes using Actuator endpoints.
examples: Input: image <your-registry>/order-service:1.2.0 → Output: 3 healthy replicas behind matching labels, receiving traffic only when ready
hints: The Deployment selector must match the pod template labels.
Use /actuator/health/liveness for liveness and /actuator/health/readiness for readiness.
Set requests for scheduling and limits as a cap, with heap sized inside the memory limit.
solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: <your-registry>/order-service:1.2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
              value: "prod"
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            limits:
              memory: "1Gi"
              cpu: "500m"
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/liveness
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/readiness
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
title: Kubernetes Deployment for Spring Boot

answer: It exits immediately, because a container lives only as long as its main process, and that process has finished.
explanation: A container's lifetime is tied to its main process. If that process is a shell that backgrounds the app and exits, the container stops, even though the backgrounded app briefly existed. The fix is to run the JVM in the foreground as the main process.
options: It keeps running, because Docker restarts background processes.
It exits immediately, because a container lives only as long as its main process, and that process has finished.
It pauses until the application is foregrounded.
It restarts in a loop until the command is changed.
prompt: A container is started with a command that launches the Java application in the background and then exits. What happens to the container, and why?
title: Container exit cause

answer: The database security group does not allow traffic from the application's security group.
explanation: In a private subnet the correct fix is a security group rule allowing the application's group as the source, not moving the database to a public subnet or using a public IP. ECS to RDS in private subnets is the standard pattern once the security group permits it.
options: The database must be moved to a public subnet.
The database security group does not allow traffic from the application's security group.
The application must use a public IP to reach the database.
RDS databases cannot be reached from ECS at all.
prompt: A Spring Boot service on ECS cannot reach its RDS database, and the database is in a private subnet. The application security group allows outbound traffic, but the database security group allows inbound PostgreSQL traffic only from a different security group. What is the most likely cause?
title: Private subnet database

description: A teammate copied a credentials file into a Docker image in one layer and deleted it in a later layer, believing the secret was gone. The image was pushed to the registry. What is the real situation, and what must the team do now?
solution: The secret is still in the image: layers are immutable, and the earlier layer containing the file remains in the image history and can be retrieved. Deleting in a later layer only hides it from the final filesystem view. The team must rotate the exposed credential immediately, rebuild the image without the secret ever being copied in, push the clean image, and remove the tainted image from the registry. Going forward, secrets arrive at run time via environment variables or a secret store, never via COPY or ENV in a Dockerfile.
title: Secret found in an image layer

description: Your team's CI pipeline fails intermittently on the same few tests, and developers have started rerunning the pipeline until it goes green. What is wrong with this habit, and what should the team do instead?
solution: Retrying until green destroys trust in CI: real failures get retried away alongside flaky ones, and the suite stops being evidence that a change is safe. The team should quarantine the flaky tests, reproduce the flakiness, and fix the root cause — usually timing assumptions, shared mutable state, test-order dependence, or reliance on an external service. Only deterministic tests return to the suite, and a pattern of retries on one test is treated as a bug to fix, not a normal workflow.
title: Flaky tests in CI

description: After a rolling update on AWS, error rates spike for a Spring Boot service, but the new containers pass their basic liveness checks. How should the team respond, and what made a fast rollback possible?
solution: Roll back first and investigate second: redeploy the previous known-good image, which the rolling update kept available, rather than hot-fixing production under pressure. Liveness only proves the process is alive, not that it serves correctly, which is why error-rate and latency alarms, readiness checks, and smoke tests matter. The rollback was possible because images are tagged by version and kept in the registry, the previous task definition or Deployment revision was retained, and configuration is separate from the image, so the old image runs correctly with current configuration.
title: Rolling back a bad AWS deployment
